blocks.text: Some of the Greek Fathers held a different view: that a female partridge, while another partridge is away, approaches its nest and so deceives the chicks by imitating the mother's voice that they leave the nest and follow her, until the true mother returns and they regret their mistake. Chrysostom reports this only in part: Ἔθος φασὶ τοὺς πέρδικας, μετὰ τὸ ἀποτεχθῆναι τῶν ὠῶν, τοὺς νεοττοὺς τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖσθαι, καὶ γυμνοῦν τὴν τεκοῦσαν [Ethos phasi tous perdikas, meta to apotechthēnai tōn ōōn, tous neottous tē phōnē proskaleisthai, kai gymnoun tēn tekousan]; They say it is the habit of partridges, after laying their eggs, to lure the chicks of others with their voice, and so rob the mother of them. But Olympiodorus says it more fully: Ὁ πέρδιξ, ὥς φασιν, ὑπερήφανος ὢν, διὰ τῆς φωνῆς τοὺς ἀλλοτρίους προσκαλεῖται νεοττοὺς, οἵτινες γνόντες ὕστερον ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν αὐτοῦ, καταλιμπάνουσιν αὐτόν [Ho perdix, hōs phasin, hyperēphanos ōn, dia tēs phōnēs tous allotrious proskaleitai neottous, hoitines gnontes hysteron hoti ouk eisin autou, katalimpanousin auton]. The partridge, as they say, being proud, entices the chicks of others with its voice; yet it is deserted by them once they have at last recognized that they are not its own. And Hippolytus most fully: Τοῦ πέρδικος κενοδόξου ζώου ὑπάρχοντος, ἐπὰν πλησίον ἴδῃ ἑτέρου πέρδικος καλιὰν νεοττοὺς ἔχουσαν, ἀποπτάντος τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὴν νομὴν, μιμούμενος τὴν τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου φωνὴν, προσκαλεῖται [II, 641] πρὸς ἑαυτὸν τοὺς νεοττούς· οἱ δὲ νεοσσοὶ, νομίσαντες τὸν ἴδιον αὐτῶν ὑπάρχειν πατέρα, προστρέχουσιν αὐτῷ· ὁ δὲ ἐγγαυριᾷ ἐν ἀλλοτρίοις τέκνοις ὡς ἰδίοις, ἐλθόντος δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου πατρὸς, καὶ βοήσαντος, τὴν ἰδίαν φωνὴν ἐπιγνόντες οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καταλιπόντες τὸν νόθον, πρὸς τὸν ἴδιον πατέρα πορεύονται [Tou perdikos kenodoxou zōou hyparchontos, epan plēsion idē heterou perdikos kalian neottous echousan, apoptantos tou patros autōn epi tēn nomēn, mimoumenos tēn tou allotriou phōnēn, proskaleitai pros heauton tous neottous; hoi de neossoi, nomisantes ton idion autōn hyparchein patera, prostrechousin autō; ho de engauria en allotriois teknois hōs idiois, elthontos de tou idiou patros, kai boēsantos, tēn idian phōnēn epignontes hoi neossoi, katalipontes ton nothon, pros ton idion patera poreuontai]. Since the partridge is a proud animal, if it sees nearby the nest of another partridge with chicks in it, while the father has flown off to feed, it lures the chicks to itself by imitating his voice. Taking it for their true father, they at once run to it. And it boasts of the chicks of another as if they were its own. But as soon as the true father has returned and called, the chicks recognize his voice, leave the spurious father, and go over to the genuine one. But I do not think these things truer than what preceded. For some charge partridges with lewdness, others with malice and cunning, but no one, as far as I know, with pride. Nor does it seem that the chicks of partridges could easily be deceived by an imitation of the mother's voice, unless one supposes them so blind that they recognize their mother by hearing alone and not also by sight. Yet even if this were granted, it would not bear on the passage of Jeremiah, in which דגר, as we have shown, does not mean to gather chicks, but eggs, to be [col. 87] brooded.

More ingenious is the view of certain Hebrews cited by Kimchi in his Lexicon: that Jeremiah was speaking only of the male partridge, which, whenever it broods eggs (and that it sometimes broods is attested by Aristotle ^{b)}, Plutarch ^{c)} and Philes ^{d)}), broods eggs that it did not itself lay, but the female did. But it is not very likely that the Prophet had this in view. For the male brooding the eggs is not peculiar to the partridge; in most birds, too, male and female sit in turn. So it is stated in the Philosopher: Ἐπωάζει δὲ τὰ πολλὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων διαδεχόμενα τὸν ἄῤῥενα τοῖς θήλεσι [Epōazei de ta polla tōn ornithōn diadechomena ton arrena tois thēlesi]. Moreover, the comparison would limp on every side if Jeremiah compared the greedy man, who seizes the goods of others, which, ill gotten, are likewise ill lost, with a male partridge brooding the eggs of its mate. For although the male broods eggs that it did not itself produce, they still cannot be called another's, since the offspring belongs as much to the father as to the mother. Nor does it do this with evil intent, like the greedy man who gapes after what belongs to others, but, as Philes says, ἐξ εὐσπλαγχνίας [ex eusplanchnias], out of a certain paternal affection and devotion towards its own. And so the matter turns out well and prosperously for it, since in this way it increases and propagates its kind. There is thus no similarity at all. Not to mention that many deny that male partridges brood eggs, according to Ulysses Aldrovandus, a recent writer, but very experienced in these matters. See him, Ornithologia book 13, ch. 17.
